transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too. Well, I guess I'm here because... things are just getting really, really frustrating for me at work lately. I'm a secondary school teacher, which I love, I really do, but as you can probably imagine, it comes with a massive amount of reading and grading. 

I came in because I'm just hitting this wall where I can sit down at my desk—usually I try to set myself up perfectly, you know, I make a cup of coffee, clear off the workspace, eliminate distractions—and I'll have this huge stack of student essays in front of me, or maybe one of those dense, fifty-page curriculum documents the district sends down that we absolutely have to review. And I sit there, fully, one hundred percent intending to just power through and get it all done. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, but within ten minutes, maybe even less sometimes, I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the entire time. Like, my eyes are physically looking at the paper, but I’m barely taking in a single word of what’s actually in front of me. Instead, my brain is just entirely somewhere else, thinking about three or four completely different things at once. I'll be worrying about an email I forgot to send to a parent, or trying to remember if I took the chicken out of the freezer, or thinking about a documentary I watched last weekend. And meanwhile, the essay is just sitting there untouched. It turns a task that should take maybe an hour into this exhausting, all-night ordeal, and I just... I can't seem to keep my brain on the page no matter how hard I try.
Have you struggled with this kind of difficulty focusing and getting distracted for most of your life, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?

No, it's definitely not a new thing. Honestly, if I really take a step back and look at it, it’s been happening for pretty much my entire life. 

Like, even way back in primary school, I can vividly remember this being a huge issue. My parents used to absolutely dread parent-teacher conferences, because it was always the exact same conversation every single year. They'd bring home my report cards, and the teachers would always write these little notes in the margins—it was almost like they were all copying from the same script. They would say things like, “He’s bright but careless,” or they’d write that I “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” Which, now that I say it out loud, is pretty much exactly what I'm dealing with at my desk right now, just without the teacher standing over my shoulder to supervise me. 

And my backpack... oh man, my backpack was an absolute disaster zone back then. My mom would try to help me organize it on Friday afternoons, and she was always—and I mean *always*—reaching down to the very bottom and pulling out these horribly crumpled, wrinkled worksheets that had just been shoved down there under old folders and broken pencils. And the most frustrating part for her, and for me too, was that a lot of the time I had actually done the work! I had sat there, forced myself to fill out the worksheet, but then the bell would ring or I'd start talking to the kid next to me, and I would just completely forget to actually walk up and turn it in to the teacher's tray. It would just get shoved into my bag and cease to exist in my mind until my parents found it a week later. 

So it was never that I didn't understand the material, hence the "bright" part of the report card, I guess, but there was just this total disconnect when it came to actually keeping my focus long enough to follow through on the whole process. So, yeah, it's definitely not a recent development. It feels like it's been this exact same pattern for as long as I can remember, it's just that the stakes are a lot higher now with my own students' essays instead of a third-grade spelling worksheet.
